title: The Sikh's service
hook: the Sikh serves, and the Guru's teaching fills the Sikh (Sukhmani 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pratipaal: the Guru's care, running ahead of the asking. Today the second stanza turns to what the Sikh does in return.

Lunchtime in the langar hall of a big gurdwara, and the food is only half the scene. Someone is rolling rotis by the hundred. Someone is stirring a pot of dal the size of a bathtub. A teenager is collecting empty plates. An older man is wiping the floor. In the shoe room by the door, someone you'll never see again is handing back your shoes, polished. They're volunteers, doing seva. Ask one of them why, and the answer might be some version of: it fills me up.
screen: `ROTIS BY THE HUNDRED.` → `YOUR SHOES, HANDED BACK POLISHED.` → `IT FILLS ME UP.`

segments.voice: The second stanza of the eighteenth ashtpadi describes the Sikh who lives in the Guru's house. In paraphrase: the servant who stays in the Guru's home accepts the Guru's command in his heart. He doesn't make a show of himself. He keeps the Name in his heart, and sells his mind to the True Guru. Then the line the stanza turns on: one who serves without desire for reward attains the Lord. The word is nihkaamee. Nih, without; kaam, desire, wanting. Serving without wanting something back: not even thanks, not even the good feeling of being seen serving. Seva done for the photo isn't quite seva yet. And here's the turn that gives today its line. Serving without wanting sounds as if it should leave a person empty. But the stanza says the opposite: the one who serves this way receives the Lord, the very thing every other kind of getting was hoping for. Yesterday the Guru filled the Sikh with the wealth of the Name. Today the Sikh's service turns out to be the open hand that wealth falls into. That's what a volunteer in the langar might mean by it fills me up. They didn't serve in order to be filled; then it wouldn't be nihkaamee. They served, and found themselves filled. Sikh tradition remembers it in stories: Guru Amar Das carrying water for Guru Angad, Bhai Lehna carrying a load of wet grass for Guru Nanak. Service first; filling follows.
screen: `LIVING IN THE GURU'S HOUSE.` · `NO SHOW OF HIMSELF.` · `NIHKAAMEE: WITHOUT WANTING.` · `THE OPEN HAND IS FILLED.` · then, large: `SERVE AND BE FILLED.`

segments.voice: Picture the people around you today, at home, at work, on your street, and look for one small need nobody has asked you to meet: a full trash can, a coworker's empty mug, a neighbor's bin left at the curb. Picture doing it without being seen, and without needing to be. Then let the picture rest, and just breathe.
Nihkaamee, without desire. Seva, service, without wanting, no show, no reward, and the stanza says it is exactly what gets filled.
Your line: serve and be filled. The open hand is the one that gets filled. Day five hundred eight, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara, cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning and minding shoes, as volunteers; Sukhmani's eighteenth ashtpadi describes service without desire for reward.

fork.setup: you notice a coworker's mug always sits empty by noon. you want to live the second stanza. what do you do?
options: fill it, and tell them you did.
fork.reveal: nihkaamee seva: service with no show and no reward. the stanza says that's exactly the hand that gets filled.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nihkaamee, without desire, serving with no wish for reward.

trapdoor: what you thought: serve others so good things come back to you.
what it means: serve without wanting anything back, and find yourself filled anyway.
what a scholar hears: the stanza's sevaa karat hoi nihkaamee, tis kau hot paraapat suaamee ties seva to attaining the Lord, a theme central to Sikh practice.
guess: serving with no wish for any reward
a vow of silence kept during service
a servant paid fairly for honest work

chat.says: Why would anyone volunteer in a kitchen for hours if they don't get anything back?
options: The stanza says one who serves wanting no reward attains the Lord; they serve, and are filled.
They do get something: the thanks and the good name that come from being seen serving.
It's a rule: every Sikh must log set hours of seva each week to stay in good standing.
chat.meaning: Nihkaamee means without desire. The second stanza says the one who serves wanting no reward, and makes no show, attains the Lord.

nihkaamee.meaning: without desire; serving with no wish for reward

langar.meaning: the free community kitchen at a gurdwara

Bhai Lehna.meaning: Guru Nanak's devoted disciple, later Guru Angad

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 18, stanza 2 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286–287)

notes: Ashtpadi 18 stanza 2 paraphrased: gur kai grihi sevak jo rahai; gur kee aagiaa man meh sahai; aapas kau kar kachh na janaavai; ... sevaa karat hoi nihkaamee, tis kau hot paraapat suaamee. Confirm the lines and the 'sells his mind' paraphrase.
Bhai Lehna carrying wet grass for Guru Nanak and Guru Amar Das carrying water: tradition, mentioned briefly.
